facts.statehood_note: Illinois's first constitution was written at Kaskaskia, which was the first state capital; the capital moved to Vandalia in 1819 and later to Springfield.
facts.nickname: The Prairie State (slogan: Land of Lincoln)
facts.name_origin: From the Miami-Illinois word irenwe·wa, meaning "he speaks the regular way." The name passed through the Ojibwe language and then French before it became "Illinois."

government.chambers: Illinois Senate (59 senators, one per Legislative District) and Illinois House of Representatives (118 representatives, two per Legislative District). Representatives serve 2-year terms; senators serve terms in a 4-year, 4-year, 2-year pattern.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The governor can sign or veto bills and can cut or remove items from spending bills; it takes a three-fifths vote in each house to override a veto. Other elected officers are the lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, comptroller, and treasurer.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Illinois (7 justices, 10-year terms). Three justices are elected from the Cook County district and one from each of the other four districts; at the end of a term a justice needs 60% of the vote in a retention election to stay. It meets in Springfield.
government.local: 102 counties. Cook County, home of Chicago, is the most populous.
government.constitution: Illinois has had four constitutions: 1818, 1848, 1870, and 1970. The current one was ratified by voters on December 15, 1970, and took effect July 1, 1971. Its bill of rights bans discrimination based on sex and on physical or mental handicap.
government.kid_line: "All men are by nature free and independent and have certain inherent and inalienable rights among which are life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness." (Illinois Constitution of 1970, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: From about 800 to 1400 CE, people of the Mississippian culture built Cahokia, a city with about 120 mounds and 10,000 to 20,000 people at its peak around 1050 to 1150. Ancestors of many Illinois Confederation tribes built earthworks like these mounds.

About a dozen independent tribes, including the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Cahokia, and Tamaroa, formed an alliance for trade, protection, and sharing resources. They lived in villages and seasonal camps where they met to trade, hunt, and gather.
A member tribe of the Illinois Confederation. Conflict in the late 1700s shrank their numbers, and in 1812 they were removed from Illinois to Missouri and Arkansas.

The Potawatomi lived in what is now northern Illinois. After treaties signed under pressure in the 1800s, most were forced west, first to a reservation in Iowa and then farther; Chief Shab-eh-nay was promised a reservation of about 1,280 acres in 1829.
The Black Hawk War of 1832, named for the Sauk leader Black Hawk, was the last armed Native resistance to white settlement in northern Illinois.

today.about: A federally recognized nation headquartered in Kansas. On April 19, 2024, the U.S. government placed about 130 acres of its Shab-eh-nay Reservation in DeKalb County into trust, making it the only federally recognized tribal nation with reservation land in Illinois; in 2025 Illinois also returned Shabbona Lake State Park (about 1,500 acres) to the nation.

first_peoples.today_note: No tribal nation is headquartered in Illinois today. The Peoria, Kaskaskia, Piankashaw, and Wea, removed in several moves to Missouri, Kansas, and Oklahoma, now form the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma. Potawatomi nations live today in Kansas (Prairie Band), Oklahoma (Citizen Band), Wisconsin (Forest County), and Michigan (Pokagon Band).
sites: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1982) with Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas (about 30 meters, or 100 feet, high)
Koster Site in the Illinois River valley, where people lived on and off for about 7,000 years
Shabbona Lake State Park in DeKalb County, named for Chief Shab-eh-nay; Illinois returned it to the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation in 2025

history.event: People begin living at the Koster Site in the Illinois River valley, one of many places where Indigenous Peoples lived for thousands of years.
Mississippian people build Cahokia, the largest early city in the region, with about 120 mounds; at its peak (about 1050 to 1150) 10,000 to 20,000 people live there.
About a dozen tribes, including the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Cahokia, and Tamaroa, form the Inoka (Illinois Confederation). The French call them the "Illinois."
French explorers Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet travel the Illinois River. In the 1680s, René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle and Henri de Tonti build forts at Starved Rock and Peoria.
The French bring slavery to the Illinois Country.
The Northwest Ordinance bans slavery in the region on paper, but it is not enforced against enslavers who already live there.
Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, a free Black man, farms and trades furs at the mouth of the Chicago River, becoming Chicago's first non-Native permanent resident.
On February 3, Congress creates Illinois Territory, with its capital at Kaskaskia. In 1812, the Kaskaskia people are removed from Illinois to Missouri and Arkansas.
Illinois writes its first constitution at Kaskaskia and on December 3 becomes the 21st state.

The 1829 Treaty of Prairie du Chien promises Potawatomi Chief Shab-eh-nay a reservation; in 1832 the Black Hawk War is fought in northern Illinois; after the 1833 Treaty of Chicago and other treaties, most Potawatomi are forced west to Iowa and then farther (the treaty lets the Pokagon Band stay in Michigan). Around 1849, the U.S. sells Shab-eh-nay's land while he is visiting family in Kansas.

Illinois's Black Laws, among the harshest in the North, limit the rights of Black residents. In Chicago, John Jones uses his home and tailor shop as stops on the Underground Railroad for freedom seekers.
Illinois sends more than 250,000 soldiers to the Union Army during the Civil War, fourth most of any state.
On February 1, Illinois becomes the first state to ratify the 13th Amendment ending slavery, and the same week it repeals most of its Black Laws.
Voters approve a new state constitution on July 2, 1870. In 1871, John Jones is elected to the Cook County Board of Commissioners.

trailblazers.name: Jean Baptiste Point du Sable
trailblazers.group: Black man, free settler and trader
trailblazers.text: Point du Sable, who called himself a "free mulatto man," farmed and traded furs at the mouth of the Chicago River from about 1788 to 1800. He was Chicago's first non-Native permanent resident and is honored as the Founder of Chicago. Scholars think his mother may have been Haitian, or that he was the son of a freed enslaved person from Kaskaskia.

trailblazers.name: Shab-eh-nay
trailblazers.text: Chief Shab-eh-nay was promised a reservation of about 1,280 acres in northern Illinois by the 1829 Treaty of Prairie du Chien. Around 1849, while he was visiting family in Kansas, the U.S. sold his land at auction. The Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation says the land was stolen; in 2024 part of it became trust land again, and in 2025 Illinois returned Shabbona Lake State Park, which is named for him.

trailblazers.name: John Jones
trailblazers.text: Born free in North Carolina, John Jones became a successful tailor in Chicago and used his home and shop as Underground Railroad stops. In 1864 he wrote a pamphlet called "The Black Laws and a Few Reasons Why They Should Be Repealed," and Illinois repealed most of those laws in 1865. In 1871 he was elected to the Cook County Board of Commissioners.

trailblazers.name: Jane Addams
trailblazers.text: Jane Addams founded Hull House in Chicago, which offered classes, clubs, and art programs to mostly immigrant neighbors. Its volunteers worked for reforms on child labor, women's right to vote, health care, and immigration.

trailblazers.name: Ida B. Wells
trailblazers.group: Black American woman journalist and suffragist
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Mississippi, Ida B. Wells became a journalist who reported on lynching. In Chicago she founded the Alpha Suffrage Club on January 30, 1913, to help Black women vote, and that June Illinois gave women the vote in presidential and local elections. She refused to march at the back of a 1913 suffrage parade and marched with the Illinois group instead.

trailblazers.name: Oscar De Priest
trailblazers.text: Oscar De Priest was elected Chicago's first African American alderman in 1915, two years after Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club to organize Black women voters. He later became the first African American elected to Congress in the 20th century.

landforms: Flat to rolling prairie plains shaped by glaciers
Charles Mound, the highest point (1,235 feet), in the Driftless Area
Driftless Area in the far northwest, never covered by glaciers
waters: Ohio River and Wabash River (southern and southeastern borders)
Lowest point (279 feet) where the Mississippi and Ohio rivers meet
geography.regions: Illinois is often divided into Northern Illinois (the Chicago area), Central Illinois, and Southern Illinois (sometimes called Little Egypt), with glacier-flattened prairie in most places and hills in the far north and far south.

ecosystems.name: Tallgrass prairie
ecosystems.about: Big bluestem, the state prairie grass, can grow stems up to eight feet tall, and milkweed (the state wildflower) feeds monarch caterpillars. The state soil, Drummer silty clay loam, is a deep, fertile prairie soil found on about 1.5 million acres.

ecosystems.name: Forests and the Shawnee Hills
ecosystems.about: Southern Illinois has forested highlands near the Shawnee National Forest. White oak is the state tree, and the white-tailed deer, chosen by schoolchildren in 1980, is the state animal.

ecosystems.name: Rivers, ponds, and wetlands
ecosystems.about: The bluegill, the state fish, is named for the bright blue gill covers of many males; painted turtles and eastern tiger salamanders also live in Illinois waters.

science.weather: Illinois has about 54 tornadoes a year on average and had 136 in 2023, the most of any state. The 1925 Tri-State Tornado killed 613 people in Illinois. Winters can bring deep snow and severe cold; the record low is -38°F (January 2019).
science.resources: Illinois farms on rich prairie soil grow large crops of corn and soybeans, helped long ago by John Deere's steel plow. Southern Illinois has coal, oil, and timber, and Illinois makes more electricity from nuclear power than any other state.
science.highlight: The Tully monster, Illinois's state fossil, has been found only in Illinois. Francis Tully found the first one in 1958. It was a soft-bodied animal about one foot long that lived in a tropical sea about 300 million years ago, with two eyelike bumps on stalks and a front arm ending in a mouthlike part with sharp points. Scientists still are not sure what kind of animal it was.

g3_ss.title: Illinois's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Springfield, Chicago, and the student's county among 102 counties; learn the 59-member Senate, 118-member House, governor, and 7-justice Supreme Court; read Article I, Section 1 of the state constitution.

g3_ss.title: Illinois's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Visit Cahokia and Monks Mound through pictures, meet the Inoka (Illinois Confederation) and the Potawatomi, and map where these nations live today.

g3_ss.title: Illinois Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, Chief Shab-eh-nay, John Jones, Jane Addams, and Ida B. Wells; students make a Chicago timeline of their lives.

g45_ss.title: Illinois's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: The Koster Site, the city of Cahokia, the Inoka (Illinois Confederation), and the Potawatomi and Sauk; treaties and removal, and the 2024 Prairie Band Potawatomi reservation.

g45_ss.title: French Illinois Country to Territory
g45_ss.plan: Marquette and Jolliet, French forts and slavery in the 1720s, the Northwest Ordinance, du Sable's Chicago, and Illinois Territory in 1809.

g45_ss.title: Free State, Black Laws, and the 13th Amendment, 1818 to 1871
g45_ss.plan: Statehood, the Black Hawk War, the Black Laws and John Jones, the Underground Railroad, 250,000 Civil War soldiers, and Illinois as first to ratify the 13th Amendment.

g3_sci.title: The Tully Monster Mystery
g3_sci.plan: Look at the state fossil, draw what it may have looked like, and talk about how scientists handle a mystery.

g3_sci.title: Prairie Plants and Animals
g3_sci.plan: Big bluestem, milkweed, and monarch butterflies; plant a mini prairie and track monarch life cycles.

g3_sci.title: Tornado Safety
g3_sci.plan: What makes a tornado, why Illinois gets so many, and how to practice a family tornado plan.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers Made the Prairie State
g45_sci.plan: How ice sheets flattened Illinois and left moraines, why the Driftless Area is hilly, and why prairie soil is so rich.

g45_sci.title: Rivers and the Great Lake
g45_sci.plan: Lake Michigan and the Mississippi, Ohio, Wabash, and Illinois rivers; map Illinois's watery borders and meet bluegill, turtles, and salamanders.

g45_sci.title: Energy in Illinois
g45_sci.plan: Coal and oil in southern Illinois and nuclear power; compare energy sources and their effects on the land.
